h.select_rule: Keep hypotheses you rate at least 55% likely true but expect other models to rate below 50%, and name the specific naive reasoning that would mislead them. Drop anything you rate below 50% yourself, and anything obvious from structure alone. Keep fields and directions diverse.
h.strategy: Propose a broad, varied set of conditional hypotheses covering many different edited fields, conditioning fields and both directions. For each, briefly note your own probability that it holds and how an intuitive reader would judge it.

hyps.why: Replacing none with a conv on the direct input-output edge adds a whole new path, whereas replacing any existing op yields only an incremental change, so the gain is larger consistently across datasets.
A skip replacing none adds a gradient highway, while a skip replacing a conv is often a downgrade, so the edit is more beneficial from none.
Pool replacing none adds a path and helps, but pool replacing a conv is a downgrade, so the edit is better from none.
A skip on the direct edge helps trainability mostly when no strong conv path reaches the output, so with a conv on edge 4 its marginal gain shrinks.
Diminishing returns: a parallel conv path into the output already supplies conv capacity, so an additional conv on edge 3 adds less.
With edge 1 removed, node 2 gets weaker and more indirect input, so a conv on edge 5 contributes less.
With edge 1 removed, node 2 carries a degraded signal, so a skip on edge 5 passes less useful information.
Edge 0 feeds edges 2 and 4 via node 1, so restoring it with a conv reactivates downstream paths and gains more than swapping one op for another.
Adding a conv to a missing final edge opens a new route into the output node, giving a larger gain than a swap.
Removing a conv from edge 4 loses real capacity, whereas removing a skip or pool, or a no-op removal, costs far less.
